question_prompt: Design an O(n² logn)-time algorithm to determine whether there exist three points in a set of n points in a 2-dimentional plane are colinear. We can assume all these n points are distinct.
gold_answer: Sort points by x, then for each point, compute slopes to all later points, sort these slopes in O(n log n) time, and check for duplicates; overall O(n² log n) due to repeated sorting.
gold_rationale: For each point, compute slopes to all later points, sort them, and check for duplicates; if found, three points are collinear. This yields \(O(n^2 \log n)\) time.
model_output:
### Rationale:
The problem requires detecting collinear points. A naive approach is O(n³). We can reduce it to O(n² logn) by fixing two points and checking if any other point lies on the line formed by them, using a sorted list for efficient searching.

### Answer:
```python
def collinear_three_points(points):
    n = len(points)
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            x1, y1 = points[i]
            x2, y2 = points[j]
            
            # Calculate slope and intercept
            if x1 == x2:
                # Vertical line
                collinear_points = [p for p in points if p[0] == x1 and p != points[i] and p != points[j]]
            else:
                slope = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1)
                intercept = y1 - slope * x1
                
                # Check for other points on the line
                collinear_points = [p for p in points if abs(p[1] - (slope * p[0] + intercept)) < 1e-6 and p != points[i] and p != points[j]]
            
            if len(collinear_points) > 0:
                return True
    return False
```
rationale_output: The problem requires detecting collinear points. A naive approach is O(n³). We can reduce it to O(n² logn) by fixing two points and checking if any other point lies on the line formed by them, using a sorted list for efficient searching.

question_prompt: For languages such as Chinese and Japanese, which are written without spaces between words, you must design an algorithm to identify likely word boundaries in a given text. Analogously, in English, this involves taking a string like "meetateight" and determining the best segmentation, such as "meet at eight". A function Quality() is provided that returns a numerical score for any string, reflecting how much it resembles a word in the language, with higher scores indicating greater word-likeness. The total quality of a segmentation is the sum of the qualities of its individual words. Design a bottom-up dynamic programming algorithm that, given a string y, finds a segmentation with the maximum total quality. Provide the recurrence relation, pseudocode, and a running time analysis, considering each call to Quality() as an O(1) operation.
gold_answer:
Let \( n \) be the length of the input string \( y \), indexed from 1 to \( n \). Define \( dp[i] \) as the maximum total quality achievable for the prefix \( y[1..i] \). The recurrence relation is:  
\[
dp[i] = \max_{1 \leq j \leq i} \left( dp[j-1] + \text{Quality}(y[j..i]) \right),
\]
with base case \( dp[0] = 0 \). The optimal segmentation is reconstructed by backtracking from \( dp[n] \).  

Pseudocode:  
```
function Segment(y):
    n = length(y)
    let dp[0..n] be an array initialized to -infinity
    dp[0] = 0
    let prev[1..n] be an array for backtracking

    for i = 1 to n:
        for j = 1 to i:
            candidate = dp[j-1] + Quality(y[j..i])
            if candidate > dp[i]:
                dp[i] = candidate
                prev[i] = j-1  // store split point before word y[j..i]

    // Reconstruction
    splits = []
    i = n
    while i > 0:
        start = prev[i] + 1
        add word y[start..i] to segmentation (from start to end)
        i = prev[i]
    reverse segmentation order
    return segmentation and dp[n]
```

Running time: \( O(n^2) \), with \( O(n) \) space for \( dp \) and \( prev \).
gold_rationale: To find the optimal segmentation maximizing total word quality, use dynamic programming: for each prefix length \( i \), compute \( dp[i] \) as the maximum over all possible last words \( y[j..i] \) of \( dp[j-1] + \text{Quality}(y[j..i]) \), with \( dp[0]=0 \). This yields an \( O(n^2) \) algorithm.

question_prompt: Explain the differences between discriminative Al and generative Al using examples?
gold_answer: Discriminative AI models classify or predict labels from data (e.g., spam detection), while generative AI models create new data similar to training data (e.g., text or image generation).
gold_rationale: Discriminative AI classifies existing data (e.g., spam filters), while generative AI creates new data (e.g., text generation). Discriminative models learn decision boundaries, whereas generative models learn data distributions to produce novel outputs.
model_output:
### Rationale:
Discriminative AI focuses on boundaries between classes, while generative AI models the data distribution itself. Discriminative models predict labels; generative models create new data instances. Examples clarify the distinction.
### Answer:
Discriminative AI learns P(Y|X) – the probability of a label Y given input X. Example: spam detection classifies emails. Generative AI learns P(X,Y) or P(X) – the joint or input probability distribution. Example: GANs creating images, LLMs generating text.
rationale_output: Discriminative AI focuses on boundaries between classes, while generative AI models the data distribution itself. Discriminative models predict labels; generative models create new data instances. Examples clarify the distinction.
answer_output: Discriminative AI learns P(Y|X) – the probability of a label Y given input X. Example: spam detection classifies emails. Generative AI learns P(X,Y) or P(X) – the joint or input probability distribution. Example: GANs creating images, LLMs generating text.

question_prompt: Explain the conceptual similarities and differences between bagging and boosting, detailing at least two essential points for each.
gold_answer: Bagging and boosting are both ensemble methods that combine multiple base models to improve predictive performance, but they differ fundamentally in how they construct and weight those models. Similarities: 1. Both use multiple weak learners (e.g., decision trees) to create a stronger ensemble model. 2. Both aim to reduce variance and/or bias compared to a single model, though their primary targets differ. Differences: 1. Training approach: Bagging trains models independently on random subsets of data (with replacement), while boosting trains models sequentially, each focusing on errors of the previous model. 2. Model weighting: Bagging typically gives equal weight to all models (e.g., averaging), whereas boosting assigns higher weight to better-performing models in the sequence.
gold_rationale: Both combine multiple weak learners to improve predictions. Bagging trains models independently on random data subsets, averaging results to reduce variance. Boosting trains sequentially, weighting models to correct errors and reduce bias.
model_output:
### Rationale:
Bagging and boosting are ensemble methods aiming to improve model accuracy. Bagging reduces variance via parallel models, while boosting reduces bias through sequential, weighted models. Key differences lie in model independence and weighting.
### Answer:
Bagging creates multiple independent models on bootstrapped datasets, averaging predictions (reducing variance). It uses parallelization and equal weighting. Boosting sequentially builds models, weighting misclassified instances to focus on difficult cases (reducing bias). It uses sequential learning and instance weighting.
rationale_output: Bagging and boosting are ensemble methods aiming to improve model accuracy. Bagging reduces variance via parallel models, while boosting reduces bias through sequential, weighted models. Key differences lie in model independence and weighting.
answer_output: Bagging creates multiple independent models on bootstrapped datasets, averaging predictions (reducing variance). It uses parallelization and equal weighting. Boosting sequentially builds models, weighting misclassified instances to focus on difficult cases (reducing bias). It uses sequential learning and instance weighting.

question_prompt: What are the advantages of Breadth First Search?
gold_answer: BFS will not get trapped exploring a blind alley. This contrasts to the DFS which may follow a single unfruitful path for a very long time, perhaps forever before the path actually terminates in a state that has no successors. If there is a solution, then BFS is guaranteed to find it. Furthermore, if there are multiple solutions then a minimal solution will be found.
gold_rationale: BFS guarantees finding a solution if one exists and yields the shortest path by exploring all nodes level by level, avoiding the risk of infinite exploration in blind alleys.
model_output:
### Rationale:
Breadth-First Search systematically explores all vertices at the present depth prior to moving on to vertices at the next depth level. This guarantees finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs and offers completeness.
### Answer:
BFS finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs. It is complete, meaning it will find a solution if one exists. BFS is useful for finding all neighbors at a given distance.
rationale_output: Breadth-First Search systematically explores all vertices at the present depth prior to moving on to vertices at the next depth level. This guarantees finding the shortest path in unweighted graphs and offers completeness.
answer_output: BFS finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs. It is complete, meaning it will find a solution if one exists. BFS is useful for finding all neighbors at a given distance.

question_prompt: Explain the mechanics of an "Invalid Curve Attack" against a server using Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH). If the server computes the shared secret $k \cdot P_{sender}$ without validating that point $P_{sender}$ is on the standard curve, what does the attacker gain?

Because $P_{sender}$ is not on the standard curve, the resulting point may reveal information about the server’s private key, $k$, allowing the attacker to recover it through techniques like rogue-curve attacks or small-subgroup attacks. Specifically, the attacker can craft $P_{sender}$ such that the scalar multiplication leaks $k$.

question_prompt: A program accesses two cache lines, one that begins at address Ox1000, and one that begins at address 0x2000. A 1-KB cache with 32-byte lines contains 32 lines and uses bits 5 through 9 of the address to select the cache line that a line of data maps into (bits O through 4 determine the byte within the line). Since the program alternates between references to each line, the line being referenced will never be in the cache, as it will have been evicted to make room for the other line. Therefore, all 200 memory references (100 to each line) will result in cache misses. The first 2 of these will be compulsory misses, and the other 198 will be conflict misses. Since the total amount of data referenced by the program is less than the capacity of the cache, no capacity misses will occur.

question_prompt: Compare lock downgrades with upgrades. Explain why downgrades violate 2PL but are nonetheless acceptable. Discuss the use of update locks in conjunction with lock downgrades.
gold_answer: A lock upgrade is to grant a transaction an exclusive lock of an object for which it already holds a shared lock. A lock downgrade happens when an exclusive lock is obtained by a transaction initially, but downgrades to a shared lock once it’s clear that this is suﬃcient. Lock downgrade violates the 2PL requirement because it reduces the locking privileges held by a transaction, and the transaction may go on to acquire other locks. But the transaction did nothing but read the object that it downgraded. So it is nonetheless acceptable, provided that the transaction has not modified the object. The downgrade approach reduces concurrency, so we introduce a new kind of lock, called an update lock, that is compatible with shared locks but not other updates and exclusive lock. By setting an update lock initially, rather than a exclusive lock as in the case of lock downgrade, we prevent conflicts with other read operations and increase concurrency.
gold_rationale: Lock downgrades reduce exclusivity (e.g., exclusive to shared) after releasing some locks, which violates strict 2PL's rule of holding all locks until commit. They are acceptable for increased concurrency. Update locks allow a transaction to later upgrade to exclusive or downgrade to shared, preventing deadlocks during the read-before-write phase.
model_output:
### Rationale: Lock downgrades and upgrades manage lock compatibility and concurrency. Downgrades don't violate 2PL's growing phase as they release more restrictive locks. Update locks facilitate safe downgrades.
### Answer: Lock upgrades involve changing a lock from a less restrictive type to a more restrictive one (e.g., S to X). Lock downgrades do the opposite (e.g., X to S). Downgrades violate the growing phase of 2PL because they release locks, but are acceptable because they do not affect the recoverability or consistency of committed transactions. Update locks are used to acquire a shared lock initially, allowing other transactions to read the data, and then upgrade to an exclusive lock when the transaction needs to modify it, enabling safe downgrades by preventing interference during the upgrade process.
rationale_output: Lock downgrades and upgrades manage lock compatibility and concurrency. Downgrades don't violate 2PL's growing phase as they release more restrictive locks. Update locks facilitate safe downgrades.
answer_output: Lock upgrades involve changing a lock from a less restrictive type to a more restrictive one (e.g., S to X). Lock downgrades do the opposite (e.g., X to S). Downgrades violate the growing phase of 2PL because they release locks, but are acceptable because they do not affect the recoverability or consistency of committed transactions. Update locks are used to acquire a shared lock initially, allowing other transactions to read the data, and then upgrade to an exclusive lock when the transaction needs to modify it, enabling safe downgrades by preventing interference during the upgrade process.

question_prompt: Explain the phases in the waterfall model with its advantages and disadvantages.
gold_answer:
Waterfall model is one of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) models. This model was devised by Royce in 1970. Since then many organizations implemented this process model and till date this is one of the majorly used software development process. The software lifecycle activities like Requirements Speciﬁcation (phase 1), Design (phase 2), Construction (phase 3), Integration (phase 4), Testing (phase 5) and Debugging (phase 6), Installation (phase 7) and Maintenance (phase 8) are proceeded one after the other (like a waterfall). So, at the beginning of the project the necessities and conditions are obtained from the customer as the ﬁrst step. This specification and analysis is the next step which is taken up by the developer team. Then the developer team will start to design a framework for achieving the objectives. Following the efficient design, the coding begins. After this, the testing process ensures the correctness of the code. Once the system is installed and launched as the live system it enters the maintenance stage. All these stages are taking place one after the other without any overlap. 
The Waterfall Model  has several advantages. It is very easy to understand and simple to implement. Since it is widely used and well known, all stakeholders can easily understand the process. In addition, the model clearly identifies deliverables and milestones at an early stage of the project.
However, the Waterfall Model also has notable disadvantages. It does not match well with real-world software development, as it is unrealistic to freeze requirements at the beginning. Software is only delivered at the final phase, which delays feedback. Furthermore, making changes is difficult and expensive, as change requests must go through the entire process.

question_prompt: Why is cache coherence a problem in shared-memory multiprocessor systems, and what general approaches exist to solve it?

General approaches to solve this include: 1) Snooping protocols (e.g., write-invalidate, write-update) where caches monitor the bus for memory transactions and update/invalidate their copies accordingly. 2) Directory-based protocols where a central directory tracks which caches hold copies of each memory block, enabling targeted updates/invalidations.
rationale_output: Cache coherence arises because multiple processors have private caches, leading to potential inconsistencies when sharing data. Solutions involve snooping protocols or directory-based protocols to maintain data consistency.

question_prompt: Explain the characteristics of SRS.
gold_answer:
Software requirements specification should be accurate, complete, efficient, and of high quality, so that it does not affect the entire project plan. An SRS is said to be of high quality when the developer and user easily understand the prepared document. Other characteristics of SRS are discussed below.
Correct: SRS is correct when all user requirements are stated in the requirements
document. The stated requirements should be according to the desired system. This implies that each requirement is examined to ensure that it (SRS) represents user requirements. Note that there is no specified tool or procedure to assure the correctness of SRS. Correctness ensures that all specified
requirements are performed correctly.
Unambiguous: SRS is unambiguous when every stated requirement has only one
interpretation. This implies that each requirement is uniquely interpreted. In case there is a term used with multiple meanings, the requirements document should specify the meanings in the SRS so that it is clear and easy to understand.
Complete: SRS is complete when the requirements clearly define what the software is required to do. This includes all the requirementsrelated to performance, design and functionality.
Ranked for importance/stability: All requirements are not equally important, hence each requirement is identified to make differences among other requirements. For this, it is essential to clearly identify each requirement. Stability implies the probability of changes in the requirement in future.
Modifiable: The requirements of the user can change, hence requirements document should
be created in such a manner that those changes can be modified easily, consistently maintaining the structure and style of the SRS.
Traceable: SRS is traceable when the source of each requirement is clear and facilitates the
reference of each requirement in future. For this, forward tracing and backward tracing are used.
Forward tracing implies that each requirement should be traceable to design and code elements.
Backward tracing implies defining each requirement explicitly referencing its source.
Verifiable: SRS is verifiable when the specified requirements can be verified with a cost-
effective process to check whether the final software meets those requirements. The requirements
are verified with the help of reviews. Note that unambiguity is essential for verifiability.
Consistent: SRS is consistent when the subsets of individual requirements defined do not
conflict with each other. For example, there can be a case when different requirements can use
different terms to refer to the same object. There can be logical or temporal conflicts between the
specified requirements and some requirements whose logical or temporal characteristics are not
satisfied. For instance, a requirement states that an event 'a' is to occur before another event 'b'. But
then another set of requirements states (directly or indirectly by transitivity) that event 'b' should
occur before event 'a'.
gold_rationale: A satisfactory answer must define SRS as a formal document specifying software requirements, covering its key characteristics: correctness, completeness, consistency, unambiguity, verifiability, modifiability, and traceability, explaining each's role in guiding development.

### Rationale: SRS (Software Requirements Specification) defines the complete behavior of the software to be developed. Key characteristics include correctness, completeness, consistency, modifiability, verifiability, traceability, and prioritisation. These ensure a clear and manageable development process.
### Answer: Correctness, completeness, consistency, modifiability, verifiability, traceability, prioritisation, and unambiguousness are SRS characteristics.

Key characteristics include correctness, completeness, consistency, modifiability, verifiability, traceability, and prioritisation. These ensure a clear and manageable development process.

question_prompt: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of the trigger mechanism. Contrast triggers with other integrity constraints supported by SQL.
gold_answer:
A trigger is a procedure that is automatically invoked in response to a specified change to the database. The advantages of the trigger mechanism include the ability to perform an action based on the result of a query condition. The set of actions that can be taken is a superset of the actions that integrity constraints can take (i.e. report an error). Actions can include invoking new update, delete, or insert queries, perform data definition statements to create new tables or views, or alter security policies. Triggers can also be executed before or after a change is made to the database (that is, use old or new data).
There are also disadvantages to triggers. These include the added complexity when
trying to match database modifications to trigger events. Also, integrity constraints
are incorporated into database performance optimization; it is more diﬃcult for a
database to perform automatic optimization with triggers. If database consistency is
the primary goal, then integrity constraints oﬀer the same power as triggers. Integrity
constraints are often easier to understand than triggers.
gold_rationale: A satisfactory answer must explain triggers' procedural flexibility and event-driven execution, contrast them with declarative constraints like CHECK and FOREIGN KEY, and discuss trade-offs in performance, complexity, and maintainability.
model_output:

Strengths include enforcing complex business rules and auditing data changes. Weaknesses are performance overhead, potential for hidden side effects, and increased database complexity. SQL supports declarative integrity constraints like PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, and CHECK constraints. These are simpler, generally more efficient, and easier to understand than triggers. Constraints define data rules directly, while triggers implement rules through code, offering greater flexibility but at the cost of maintainability and potential performance issues.
rationale_output: Triggers offer procedural integrity enforcement, reacting to data changes. They are powerful but can impact performance and introduce complexity. Compared to declarative constraints, triggers are more flexible but harder to manage.

The innermost track on a hard disk platter has a radius of 0.25 in (i.e., is located at
0.25 in from the center of the spindle). The outermost track has a radius of 1.75 in.
What is the ratio of the capacity of the disk if a variable number of tracks per sector is used compared to the capacity if a fixed number of tracks/ sector is used? In the fixed number of sectors/track scheme, the number of sectors on each track is determined by the number that can be fit on the innermost track, and all tracks have the same capacity. Using a variable number of sectors per track, the amount of space a sector takes up on a track will be the same for all tracks, so the ratio of the capacity of the average track to that of the innermost track is equal to the ratio of the length of the average track to the length of the innermost track.
Since the capacity of each track in the fixed number of sectors scheme is the same as the capacity of the innermost track, this ratio will be the ratio of the total capacities of the two schemes. Circumference is linear with radius, so the average-length track will be the one halfway between the innermost and outermost tracks. The innermost track has a radius of 0.25 in, and the outermost has a ratio of 1.75 in, for a difference of 1.5 in. The ratio of the circumferences of two tracks is the same as the ratio of their radii, so the average track will have 4 times the capacity of the innermost track, and the variable-number-of-sectors scheme will give 4 times as much capacity on the disk as the fixed-number-of-sectors scheme.

question_prompt: Explain the concept of multithreading in modern CPU architectures, highlighting its relationship with multiprocessing and detailing its primary advantages and disadvantages.
gold_answer:
Multithreading is the ability of a central processing unit (CPU) or a single core in a
multi-core processor to execute multiple processes or threads concurrently, appropriately
supported by the operating system. This approach differs from multiprocessing, as with
multithreading the processes and threads share the resources of a single or multiple cores: the
computing units, the CPU caches, and the translation lookaside buffer (TLB).
Where multiprocessing systems include multiple complete processing units, multithreading
aims to increase utilization of a single core by using thread-level as well as instruction-level
parallelism. As the two techniques are complementary, they are sometimes combined in
systems with multiple multithreading CPUs and in CPUs with multiple multithreading cores.
Advantages: If a thread gets a lot of cache misses, the other threads can continue taking advantage of the unused computing resources, which may lead to faster overall execution as these resources would have been idle if only a single thread were executed. Also, if a thread cannot use all the computing resources of the CPU (because instructions depend on each other's
result), running another thread may prevent those resources from becoming idle. If several threads work on the same set of data, they can actually share their cache, leading to better cache usage or synchronization on its values. Disadvantages: Multiple threads can interfere with each other when sharing hardware resources such as caches or translation lookaside buffers (TLBs). As a result, execution times of a single thread are not improved but can be degraded, even when only one thread is executing, due to lower frequencies or additional pipeline stages that are necessary to accommodate thread-switching hardware.
gold_rationale: A satisfactory answer must define multithreading, contrast it with multiprocessing, explain its resource-sharing nature, and discuss at least one advantage and disadvantage, such as improved resource utilization versus potential interference and performance overhead.

Advantages include improved responsiveness and resource sharing, while disadvantages involve increased complexity and potential for contention.
### Answer: Multithreading allows a single CPU core to handle multiple execution contexts (threads) concurrently. Unlike multiprocessing, which employs multiple physical cores, multithreading creates the illusion of parallelism on a single core by rapidly switching between threads. Advantages include increased CPU utilization, improved responsiveness (especially for I/O-bound tasks), and reduced overhead compared to process creation. Disadvantages include increased complexity in programming and debugging, potential for thread contention leading to performance degradation, and the limitation that true parallelism is not achieved without multiple cores.

question_prompt: Describe the use of locks for improved conflict resolution in Optimistic Concurrency Control.
gold_answer: In Optimistic Concurrency Control, we have no way to tell when T_i wrote the object at the time we validate T_j, since all we have is the list of objects written by T_i and the list read by T_j. To solve such conflict, we use mechanisms very similar to locking. The basic idea is that each transaction in the Read phase tells the DBMS about items it is reading, and when a transaction T_i is committed and its writes are accepted, the DBMS checks whether any of the items written by T_i are being rad by any (yet to be validated) transaction T_j. If so, we know that T_j’s validation must eventually fail. Then we can pick either the die or kill policy to resolve the conflict.
gold_rationale: Locks are used in OCC's validation phase to temporarily serialize conflicting transactions, ensuring atomicity of the commit check and preventing the lost update problem that can occur with pure timestamp-based validation.
model_output:
### Rationale: Optimistic concurrency control avoids locking during transactions. However, locks are used during the validation phase to ensure that changes can be applied without violating serializability. This prevents lost updates.
### Answer: In optimistic concurrency control, locks are applied *during validation*, not throughout the transaction. A read lock is acquired on data being written to confirm no conflicting updates occurred since the data was read. If the lock cannot be acquired, the transaction is rolled back.
rationale_output: Optimistic concurrency control avoids locking during transactions. However, locks are used during the validation phase to ensure that changes can be applied without violating serializability. This prevents lost updates.
answer_output: In optimistic concurrency control, locks are applied *during validation*, not throughout the transaction. A read lock is acquired on data being written to confirm no conflicting updates occurred since the data was read. If the lock cannot be acquired, the transaction is rolled back.

question_prompt: Explain the core mechanic of the KRACK (Key Reinstallation Attack) against WPA2. How does replaying Message 3 of the 4-way handshake compromise encryption without knowing the password?
gold_answer: KRACK does not steal the password. Instead, it targets the handshake state machine. By replaying Message 3, the attacker tricks the client into reinstalling the already-negotiated session key. The protocol specification dictates that when a key is installed, the transmit counters (Nonce) must be reset to zero. This nonce reset, while using the same encryption key, leads to "Nonce Reuse." This allows the attacker to decrypt packets (keystream reuse) or forge packets, bypassing the encryption layer.
gold_rationale: KRACK exploits the 4-way handshake by forcing a client to reinstall an already-in-use encryption key. This resets the packet number counter, allowing an attacker to replay and decrypt packets without needing the password.
model_output:
### Rationale:
KRACK exploits vulnerabilities in the WPA2 protocol's 4-way handshake. Specifically, it manipulates the third message, forcing reinstallation of the encryption key, enabling decryption of traffic without the password.
### Answer:
KRACK compromises WPA2 by exploiting a flaw in the 4-way handshake. An attacker replays the third message (containing an encrypted Transition Confirmation Key - TK) of the handshake. This forces the client to reinstall the previously used TK, resulting in the same key being used for multiple data transmissions. Because the nonce used in the encryption is reused with the same key, a stream cipher like CCMP becomes vulnerable to key reuse attacks, allowing decryption of captured traffic without knowing the WPA2 password.
rationale_output: KRACK exploits vulnerabilities in the WPA2 protocol's 4-way handshake. Specifically, it manipulates the third message, forcing reinstallation of the encryption key, enabling decryption of traffic without the password.

question_prompt: Explain why miss rate is not a good metric for evaluating cache memory performance.
gold_answer:
The average access time in a cache memory system is given by: T_avg = T_hit + mT_miss
A cache memory may have low miss rate (m), but a high access time (Thit), making it have lower performance than one with a higher miss rate.
gold_rationale: Miss rate alone ignores access time and cost; a low miss rate may come from a large, slow cache that degrades overall performance. A satisfactory answer must mention trade-offs with hit time, cost, and alternative metrics like AMAT.

### Rationale:
Miss rate only considers whether a memory access misses the cache, not the time penalty. Hit time is crucial; a low miss rate with a high hit time can be worse than a higher miss rate with a low hit time. Therefore, average memory access time (AMAT) is a better metric.
### Answer:
Miss rate doesn't account for hit time. A low miss rate with a large hit time can result in poor performance. AMAT, considering both hit and miss penalties, provides a more accurate evaluation of cache performance.
rationale_output: Miss rate only considers whether a memory access misses the cache, not the time penalty. Hit time is crucial; a low miss rate with a high hit time can be worse than a higher miss rate with a low hit time. Therefore, average memory access time (AMAT) is a better metric.

question_prompt: Explain different types of Requirements with example.
gold_answer:
Requirements can be categorized into 3 main types: Functional (User) Requirements, Non Functional (System) Requirements, Interface Specification.
Functional (User) Requirements: The set of requirements which deﬁne what the system will do or accomplish are called functional requirements. These are the requirements which determine how the software will behave to meet certain user needs. The requirements may be for performing some calculation, data manipulation, processing, logical decision making etc. which form the basis of the business rules. Functional requirements are often captured as Use Cases. Functional requirements are the main driver for the Application Architecture of the system. An example of functional requirement is – a retail shop billing software must have the functionalities of capturing commodity prices, calculate the discounts, generate the bill, print the invoice etc.
Non Functional (System) Requirements: Functional requirements are supported by Non-functional requirements. The quality attributes and the design and architecture constraints that the system must have are called the Non-functional requirements.
Some of the quality attributes of the system from end user's vie are: Performance, availability, usability and Security.
Some of the system quality attribute from developer's view are : Reusability, testability, maintainability, portability.
Non functional (system) requirements are critical in most of the software projects than the functional requirements. Non functional Requirements cater to the architectural needs of the overall system where as functional requirements caters to the design needs of the overall system.
Non functional requirements may be related to the product or organization or the external requirements of the system.
Examples for Product related non functional requirements are : Performance, availability, maintainability, portability, reliability, security, scalability, testability, usability.
Examples for Organization related non functional requirements are : Standards requirements , Implementation requirements.
Examples for External non functional requirements are : Legal Requirements , Ethical requirements.
Example of non-functional requirements are :
'The system should be available 24X7' (Availability)
"The system should save or fetch 1000 records in 1 second' etc. (Performance)
Interface Specification: Most of the software systems don't work alone and in order to work those need to interact with other systems. They interact with many other systems to receive and send data, get help in processing logic, store information in other systems and for other reasons. The interaction requirement of one system with another is defined in the Interface specification.
This helps in building different systems in such a fashion that they can seamlessly interact with each other to produce the desired outcome. In our previous example of the retail shop billing system may interact with another system - an inventory system to make sure that the warehouse keeps track of the stock of the material at hand and the protocol of how these two systems interact with each other are captured in the interface specification document.

question_prompt: Explain the mechanics of the JWT "Key Confusion" (or Algorithm Confusion) attack. How does an attacker exploit a server that supports both HS256 (HMAC) and RS256 (RSA) to forge a token?
gold_answer: In this attack, the attacker changes the JWT header algorithm from RS256 to HS256. They then sign the token using the server's Public Key as the HMAC secret. If the server implementation creates the verifier based on the header's alg field, it will switch to HMAC verification but use its configured verification key (the Public Key) as the shared secret. Since the Public Key is known to the attacker, they can generate a valid HMAC signature that the server accepts.
gold_rationale: A satisfactory answer must explain that the attacker modifies the token header to specify the HS256 algorithm, then signs it with the public RSA key, which the server mistakenly uses as an HMAC secret key for verification, leading to token forgery.
model_output:
### Rationale:
The Key Confusion attack exploits servers incorrectly handling JWT algorithms. Attackers forge tokens by using the RS256 algorithm with a public key where HS256 is expected, bypassing signature verification. This relies on the server's flawed algorithm processing.
### Answer:
The JWT Key Confusion attack occurs when a server accepts both HS256 and RS256 for JWT verification but doesn't properly validate the key type based on the algorithm. An attacker crafts a JWT with the `alg` header set to `RS256`. However, instead of using a public key for verification, they use the secret key (intended for HS256). Because RS256 verification with the secret key effectively performs an HMAC operation, and the server incorrectly assumes a public key is being used, the signature is accepted as valid, allowing the attacker to forge tokens. The server fails to distinguish between the expected RSA signature and the HMAC-like result.
rationale_output: The Key Confusion attack exploits servers incorrectly handling JWT algorithms. Attackers forge tokens by using the RS256 algorithm with a public key where HS256 is expected, bypassing signature verification. This relies on the server's flawed algorithm processing.

The server fails to distinguish between the expected RSA signature and the HMAC-like result.

question_prompt: Discuss key steps for Software Configuration Management (SCM).
gold_answer:
Software Configuration Management has four key steps that must be defined for each software project to ensure a good SCM process is implemented. These are Configuration Identification, Configuration Control, Configuration Status Accounting, Configuration Authentication.
Configuration Identiﬁcation: Software is usually made up of several programs. Each program, its related documentation and data is termed as a "conﬁgurable item" (CI). The number of CI in any software project and the grouping of artifacts that make up a CI is a decision made by the project team.
Conﬁguration Control: The process of coordinating the approved changes for the proposed CIs and implementing the changes on the appropriate baseline are called Configuration control.
Conﬁguration Status Accounting: Conﬁguration status accounting is the book keeping process of each release. This procedure involves tracking what is in each version of software and the changes that lead to this version. Conﬁguration status accounting keeps a record of all the changes made to the previous baseline to reach a new baseline.
Configuration Authentication: Conﬁguration authentication (CA) is the process of assuring that the new baseline has incorporated all the planned and approved changes. The process involves verifying that all the functional aspects of the software are complete and it also verifies whether the delivery is complete in terms of the right programs, documentation and data being delivered. The conﬁguration authentication is an audit which is performed on the delivery before it is opened to the entire world.
gold_rationale: A satisfactory answer must cover core SCM activities: version control, change management, build/release management, and status accounting, explaining their purpose in maintaining software integrity and enabling team collaboration throughout the development lifecycle.
